skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/claude-stack-doctor

# Claude Stack Doctor

One command surfaces every known silent-failure class in the automation/memory stack. Run it before debugging anything by hand.

## Quick start

```powershell
pwsh -NoProfile -File "$HOME\.claude\skills\claude-stack-doctor\scripts\stack-check.ps1"
```

Exit 0 = all clear. Exit 1 = the VERDICT line lists issue codes. Report the findings to the user, then apply the matching fix below.

## Weekly scheduled run

Task Scheduler job `KeystoneOS-StackDoctor` (Mondays 6:40 AM, added 2026-07-16) runs `scripts/weekly-check.ps1`: the same read-only check, unattended. On failure it appends a one-line summary to `~\.claude\global-memory\transcripts\.errors.log` (surfaced at every session start per CLAUDE.md) and the full output is always in `scripts/last-weekly-run.log`. When a session surfaces such an entry, run this skill interactively to diagnose and fix, then clear the entry from `.errors.log`.

## Known failure classes and fixes

These four classes have each bitten more than once (evidence: daily logs 2026-04 → 2026-07). Match the issue code to its fix:

### `task:*` / `task-stale:*` — scheduled task failed or didn't run
1. Read the `action:` line the script printed and run that exact command **manually in a foreground terminal** — Task Scheduler swallows errors; foreground shows them.
2. Known root causes: executable referenced without full path (Task Scheduler has minimal PATH — always use full paths like `C:\Program Files\PowerShell\7\pwsh.exe`); venv deleted by a Python migration (see below).
3. A task failing with code 1 but no output usually means the script's own logging is the only evidence — check for a `*.log` next to the script.

### `venv-missing` / `venv-broken` — Python venv rot
Root cause seen twice: **Windows Python Install Manager migrations delete `C:\Python31x`**, orphaning every venv and pip shim built on it (killed morning-briefing silently for 6 days, 6/12–6/17; broke memsearch.exe 6/11).
Fix: recreate the venv (`python -m venv .venv` + reinstall from the project's requirements/pyproject), then manually run the dependent scheduled task once to confirm.

### `memsearch-path` / `memsearch-run` — memsearch CLI broken
- Not on PATH or exe errors → the pip shim at `%APPDATA%\Python\Python31x\Scripts\memsearch.exe` has a hardcoded stale interpreter path. Reinstall: `pip install --force-reinstall memsearch`.
- **After ANY pip upgrade/reinstall of memsearch, the local flush patch is stripped** — this is the known cause of `.errors.log` entries. Re-apply the patch (see the compiler repo's notes at `~\.claude\claude-memory-compiler\`), then confirm `.errors.log` stays empty for a session.

### `errors-log` / `flush-stale` / `flush-error` / `flush-missing` — memory pipeline
- `.errors.log` non-empty → read the entries; most common is the stripped memsearch flush patch (above) or an Agent SDK timeout ("Control request timeout: initialize" — transient, but recurring daily means the hook environment is broken).
- `last-flush.json` stale >48h → the Stop/SessionEnd hooks aren't firing; check `~\.claude\claude-memory-compiler\scripts\flush.log` tail for the real error.
- FLUSH_ERROR in dailies → same investigation; `flush.log` is ground truth.

### `backup-*` — daily backup rot (added 2026-07-23, system audit Phase 2)
The scheduled task `KeystoneOS-DailyBackup` (daily 6:15 AM) runs `~\.claude\scripts\daily-backup.ps1`: auto-commits+pushes the memory repos (SecondBrain, dotclaude, claude-skills, claude-global-memory), robocopy-snapshots `~\.claude\projects`, `~\.codex`, `~\.gemini` (→ personal Google Drive `G:\My Drive\Backups\Machine`) and non-repo DEV folders (→ Baylor OneDrive), runs an uncapped full memsearch reindex (added 7/24 — absorbs heavy-day backlogs the 45s SessionEnd hook can't; the SecondBrain library first-index is an hours-scale one-time cost that converges across nights), and resets the hook's timeout-streak counter. Restore procedure: `~\.claude\RESTORE.md`.
- `backup-missing` / `backup-stale` → task didn't run; re-run the script foreground: `pwsh -NoProfile -File ~\.claude\scripts\daily-backup.ps1`
- `backup-error` → read `~\.claude\scripts\logs\daily-backup.log`; a `repo-diverged:*` entry means a memory repo has both remote and local changes — reconcile manually (the script refuses to merge from automation).
- `backup-repo-drift:*` → pushes failing (>3 unpushed commits); usually gh/git auth rot — run `gh auth status`.
- `backup-cloud-*` → the Drive-API heartbeat (gws CLI queries RESTORE.md's cloud modifiedTime). `-check` = gws auth rot (re-auth needs explicit full scope URLs: `gws auth login --scopes "https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/calendar.readonly"` — full drive read/write per Eric's 7/24 request; the `-s drive` shorthand silently grants NO scopes, v0.22.5 bug; after re-auth delete `~\.config\gws\token_cache.json`, it serves the stale token otherwise; the login is interactive — Eric must run it via `!` and be AT the machine, then open the printed URL via Start-Process, never terminal copy/paste which truncates at line-wrap). `-stale`/`-missing` = files reach local G: cache but Google Drive for Desktop isn't syncing — check GoogleDriveFS is running and signed in.

## Not covered by the script (check manually if symptoms point there)

- **MCP/plugin auth rot** (9 manual fix-it sessions on record): run `claude doctor` / `claude mcp list` and re-auth any claude.ai connectors showing failures (Supabase, Vercel, Google Calendar have all rotted before).
- **Catapult OpenField token expiry**: see the auth section of `pp-catapult-openfield-connect`.

## Rules

- Read-only by default: the script never mutates state. Fixes are applied by you, deliberately, after reporting findings.
- Don't assume the obvious culprit — a signal that pattern-matches a known failure may have a different cause (lesson: 6/25 Milvus/ETIMEDOUT misdiagnosis). Confirm with the foreground re-run before fixing.
- When a fix is applied, re-run the script to verify the issue code clears, and note the incident in memory if it's a new failure class.

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

When multiple skills apply, process skills come first — they set the approach, then implementation skills (frontend-design, etc.) carry it out. Brainstorming and systematic-debugging are Superpowers' most common process skills, but the rule holds for any of them.

- **`-DryRun` cannot verify a write path.** It passes `rsync -n`, which writes nothing. A
  snapshot that fails live will show `OK` in a dry run. Only a non-dry run is evidence.
- **`snapshot:sessions` was never a lock or permission fault.** `~/.codex/sessions` is
  ~289 MB and had never been fully seeded into DriveFS. A live run on 2026-08-14 showed
  rsync copying steadily but slowly (~47 MB in 78 min — DriveFS throttles writes), so the
  nightly run was simply not finishing. Expect the first full seed to take hours and to

  two backup layers: the Drive SNAP of `~/.claude/projects`, and the SSD. With CRASHBOX
  unmounted that is a single copy. Nothing to "commit" there — it's by design.

The nightly backup is `~/.claude/scripts/daily-backup.ps1` (pwsh, launchd
`com.keystone.dailybackup`), driven by `~/.claude/scripts/backup-manifest.json`, logging to
`~/.claude/scripts/logs/daily-backup.log`. `~/.claude` is itself the `dotclaude` repo.
Workflow docs live in `~/DEV/Bucket` (`docs/SYSTEM-HEALTH-FINDINGS.md`,
`docs/AGENT-FIX-PROMPT.md`, `docs/FIX-STATUS-2026-08-14.md`).

## The root cause behind most "divergence" symptoms

The retired **Windows box still runs `daily-backup.ps1` and pushes to the shared repos**
(SecondBrain, dotclaude, claude-skills, claude-global-memory). Two writers on one set of
repos manufactures `repo-diverged:SecondBrain` nightly. Confirmed by the commit-message
format `chore: daily backup sync YYYY-MM-DD [auto]`, generated at `daily-backup.ps1:62` —
the VPS's `nightly-push.sh` does not produce that string, so the writer is a machine
running the PowerShell script.

**Reconciling on the Mac buys one night.** The permanent fix is Prompt 2 in
`Bucket/docs/AGENT-FIX-PROMPT.md`, run on the Windows machine (final sync, then
`Disable-ScheduledTask` — disable, never unregister). Not reachable from the Mac.

## Manifest classification — get this right, it routes athlete data

`backup-manifest.json` is default-deny: any `~/DEV` dir absent from `paths[]` fails the
health check. Adding an entry requires a human class call:

| class | destinations |
|---|---|
| `institutional` | `ssd`, `baylor` (+`github` if a repo) |
| `personal` | `ssd` (+`github` if a repo) |

`isRepo: true` also sets `captureOrphans` and `captureWorkingTree` true and needs `remote`.
**Athlete data must never be classed `personal`** — `personal` skips the Baylor OneDrive
destination. `baylor` is `deprecated: true` and must never be a sole destination.

## Traps that cost time

- **Milvus is NOT in the memsearch path**, despite what `RESTORE.md` and the Bucket docs
  say. Indexing works with port 19530 closed and Docker not installed. Don't set it up.
- **`-DryRun` cannot verify a write path.** It passes `rsync -n`, which writes nothing. A
  snapshot that fails live will show `OK` in a dry run. Only a non-dry run is evidence.
- **`daily-backup.ps1` refuses to merge diverged repos by design** — that's correct
  behavior, not a bug. Reconcile by hand.
- **stack-doctor's cloud heartbeat** watches the newest per-run receipt
  (`_receipts/run-*.txt`). It used to watch `RESTORE.md`, which the job *copies*
  (`Copy-Item -Force`, line 411) rather than rewrites, so its mtime never advanced and the
  check cried `backup-cloud-stale (218h)` while DriveFS was healthy. Fixed 2026-08-14.
- **Untracked files block a fast-forward**, and plain `git stash` does not pick them up —
  needs `-u`, or rename them aside. Bit the documented SecondBrain fix.
- Reading exit codes through a pipe returns the *last* pipeline element's status, not the
  command's — see [[project-zsh-shell-traps]]. This produced two wrong readings in one
  session (`rsync ... | tail` and a stack-check run).

## Standing state as of 2026-08-14

Fixed: `Invoke-Rsync` false-OK guard, 6 manifest entries, SecondBrain reconciled (both
machines' briefings preserved, Mac copies renamed `*.mac-local.md`), stack-doctor cloud
heartbeat. Morning brief **retired** at Eric's request — `com.keystone.morningbriefing`
booted out + disabled, plist and `~/DEV/morning-briefing` retained, dropped from
stack-doctor's checked sets. `com.keystone.morning` is a *different* KeystoneOS cadence —
leave it alone.

Open: the Windows writer (above); CRASHBOX SSD unmounted, so gitignored data and
working-tree edits have no backup; `codex/sessions` snapshot unconfirmed in a live write.

health check. Adding an entry requires a human class call:

|---|---|

The nightly backup is `~/.claude/scripts/daily-backup.ps1` (pwsh, launchd
`com.keystone.dailybackup`), driven by `~/.claude/scripts/backup-manifest.json`, logging to
`~/.claude/scripts/logs/daily-backup.log`. `~/.claude` is itself the `dotclaude` repo.
Workflow docs live in `~/DEV/Bucket` (`docs/SYSTEM-HEALTH-FINDINGS.md`,
`docs/AGENT-FIX-PROMPT.md`, `docs/FIX-STATUS-2026-08-14.md`).

## The root cause behind most "divergence" symptoms

The retired **Windows box still runs `daily-backup.ps1` and pushes to the shared repos**
(SecondBrain, dotclaude, claude-skills, claude-global-memory). Two writers on one set of
repos manufactures `repo-diverged:SecondBrain` nightly. Confirmed by the commit-message
format `chore: daily backup sync YYYY-MM-DD [auto]`, generated at `daily-backup.ps1:62` —
the VPS's `nightly-push.sh` does not produce that string, so the writer is a machine
running the PowerShell script.

**Reconciling on the Mac buys one night.** The permanent fix is Prompt 2 in
`Bucket/docs/AGENT-FIX-PROMPT.md`, run on the Windows machine (final sync, then
`Disable-ScheduledTask` — disable, never unregister). Not reachable from the Mac.

## Manifest classification — get this right, it routes athlete data

`backup-manifest.json` is default-deny: any `~/DEV` dir absent from `paths[]` fails the
health check. Adding an entry requires a human class call:

| class | destinations |
|---|---|
| `institutional` | `ssd`, `baylor` (+`github` if a repo) |
| `personal` | `ssd` (+`github` if a repo) |

`isRepo: true` also sets `captureOrphans` and `captureWorkingTree` true and needs `remote`.
**Athlete data must never be classed `personal`** — `personal` skips the Baylor OneDrive
destination. `baylor` is `deprecated: true` and must never be a sole destination.

## Traps that cost time

- **Milvus is NOT in the memsearch path**, despite what `RESTORE.md` and the Bucket docs
  say. Indexing works with port 19530 closed and Docker not installed. Don't set it up.
- **`-DryRun` cannot verify a write path.** It passes `rsync -n`, which writes nothing. A
  snapshot that fails live will show `OK` in a dry run. Only a non-dry run is evidence.
- **`snapshot:sessions` was never a lock or permission fault.** `~/.codex/sessions` is
  ~289 MB and had never been fully seeded into DriveFS. A live run on 2026-08-14 showed
  rsync copying steadily but slowly (~47 MB in 78 min — DriveFS throttles writes), so the
  nightly run was simply not finishing. Expect the first full seed to take hours and to
  span several nights; rsync resumes where it left off. Don't chase excludes for it.
- **Tier A memory is NOT in git.** `~/.claude/.gitignore` line 1 is `/*` (default-deny
  allowlist) and `projects/` is not allowlisted, so `projects/*/memory/*.md` has exactly
  two backup layers: the Drive SNAP of `~/.claude/projects`, and the SSD. With CRASHBOX
  unmounted that is a single copy. Nothing to "commit" there — it's by design.
- **`daily-backup.ps1` refuses to merge diverged repos by design** — that's correct
  behavior, not a bug. Reconcile by hand.
- **stack-doctor's cloud heartbeat** watches the newest per-run receipt
  (`_receipts/run-*.txt`). It used to watch `RESTORE.md`, which the job *copies*
  (`Copy-Item -Force`, line 411) rather than rewrites, so its mtime never advanced and the
  check cried `backup-cloud-stale (218h)` while DriveFS was healthy. Fixed 2026-08-14.
- **Untracked files block a fast-forward**, and plain `git stash` does not pick them up —
  needs `-u`, or rename them aside. Bit the documented SecondBrain fix.
- Reading exit codes through a pipe returns the *last* pipeline element's status, not the
  command's — see [[project-zsh-shell-traps]]. This produced two wrong readings in one
  session (`rsync ... | tail` and a stack-check run).

## The root cause behind most "divergence" symptoms

The retired **Windows box still runs `daily-backup.ps1` and pushes to the shared repos**
(SecondBrain, dotclaude, claude-skills, claude-global-memory). Two writers on one set of
repos manufactures `repo-diverged:SecondBrain` nightly. Confirmed by the commit-message
format `chore: daily backup sync YYYY-MM-DD [auto]`, generated at `daily-backup.ps1:62` —
the VPS's `nightly-push.sh` does not produce that string, so the writer is a machine
running the PowerShell script.

`Bucket/docs/AGENT-FIX-PROMPT.md`, run on the Windows machine (final sync, then
`Disable-ScheduledTask` — disable, never unregister). Not reachable from the Mac.

## Manifest classification — get this right, it routes athlete data

`backup-manifest.json` is default-deny: any `~/DEV` dir absent from `paths[]` fails the
health check. Adding an entry requires a human class call:

| class | destinations |
|---|---|
| `institutional` | `ssd`, `baylor` (+`github` if a repo) |
| `personal` | `ssd` (+`github` if a repo) |

`isRepo: true` also sets `captureOrphans` and `captureWorkingTree` true and needs `remote`.
**Athlete data must never be classed `personal`** — `personal` skips the Baylor OneDrive
destination. `baylor` is `deprecated: true` and must never be a sole destination.

## Traps that cost time

- **Milvus is NOT in the memsearch path**, despite what `RESTORE.md` and the Bucket docs
  say. Indexing works with port 19530 closed and Docker not installed. Don't set it up.
- **`-DryRun` cannot verify a write path.** It passes `rsync -n`, which writes nothing. A
  snapshot that fails live will show `OK` in a dry run. Only a non-dry run is evidence.
- **`snapshot:sessions` was never a lock or permission fault.** `~/.codex/sessions` is
  ~289 MB and had never been fully seeded into DriveFS. A live run on 2026-08-14 showed
  rsync copying steadily but slowly (~47 MB in 78 min — DriveFS throttles writes), so the
  nightly run was simply not finishing. Expect the first full seed to take hours and to
  span several nights; rsync resumes where it left off. Don't chase excludes for it.
- **Tier A memory is NOT in git.** `~/.claude/.gitignore` line 1 is `/*` (default-deny
  allowlist) and `projects/` is not allowlisted, so `projects/*/memory/*.md` has exactly
  two backup layers: the Drive SNAP of `~/.claude/projects`, and the SSD. With CRASHBOX
  unmounted that is a single copy. Nothing to "commit" there — it's by design.
- **`daily-backup.ps1` refuses to merge diverged repos by design** — that's correct
  behavior, not a bug. Reconcile by hand.
- **stack-doctor's cloud heartbeat** watches the newest per-run receipt
  (`_receipts/run-*.txt`). It used to watch `RESTORE.md`, which the job *copies*
  (`Copy-Item -Force`, line 411) rather than rewrites, so its mtime never advanced and the
  check cried `backup-cloud-stale (218h)` while DriveFS was healthy. Fixed 2026-08-14.
- **Untracked files block a fast-forward**, and plain `git stash` does not pick them up —
  needs `-u`, or rename them aside. Bit the documented SecondBrain fix.
- Reading exit codes through a pipe returns the *last* pipeline element's status, not the
  command's — see [[project-zsh-shell-traps]]. This produced two wrong readings in one
  session (`rsync ... | tail` and a stack-check run).

## Standing state as of 2026-08-14

Fixed: `Invoke-Rsync` false-OK guard, 6 manifest entries, SecondBrain reconciled (both
machines' briefings preserved, Mac copies renamed `*.mac-local.md`), stack-doctor cloud
heartbeat. Morning brief **retired** at Eric's request — `com.keystone.morningbriefing`
booted out + disabled, plist and `~/DEV/morning-briefing` retained, dropped from
stack-doctor's checked sets. `com.keystone.morning` is a *different* KeystoneOS cadence —
leave it alone.

CRASHBOX SSD **reattached 2026-08-14 ~11:50** (`/Volumes/CRASHBOX/AssistantBackup`, 447 GB
free, writable) — first orphan/working-tree capture since migration should appear in the
next nightly log. Bucket doc set committed + pushed (`ce94371`).

Open: the Windows writer (above) — the last thing manufacturing nightly divergence;
`codex/sessions` first seed still filling (write path proven working — see traps).
`.errors.log` retains 6 historical lines; clear the file once the Windows writer is
retired and the seed completes, not before — conditions named in it are still live.

Note the run ordering: Drive SNAPs run *before* the SSD capture, so a long `codex/sessions`
seed delays the SSD layer within a given run. Not a failure, just a wait.

name: backup-sync-system
description: "Nightly backup/sync architecture and its traps — two-writer root cause, manifest classification rules, Milvus is NOT in the memsearch path, dry-run can't verify writes"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 3db720f8-cca5-4aed-96cd-e7ac4a95ab2d
  modified: 2026-08-14T19:27:48.356Z
---

The nightly backup is `~/.claude/scripts/daily-backup.ps1` (pwsh, launchd
`com.keystone.dailybackup`), driven by `~/.claude/scripts/backup-manifest.json`, logging to
`~/.claude/scripts/logs/daily-backup.log`. `~/.claude` is itself the `dotclaude` repo.
Workflow docs live in `~/DEV/Bucket` (`docs/SYSTEM-HEALTH-FINDINGS.md`,
`docs/AGENT-FIX-PROMPT.md`, `docs/FIX-STATUS-2026-08-14.md`).

## The root cause behind most "divergence" symptoms — CLOSED 2026-08-14

The retired **Windows box was still running `daily-backup.ps1` and pushing to the shared
repos** (SecondBrain, dotclaude, claude-skills, claude-global-memory). Two writers on one
set of repos manufactured `repo-diverged:SecondBrain` nightly. Identified by the
commit-message format `chore: daily backup sync YYYY-MM-DD [auto]`, generated at
`daily-backup.ps1:62`.

**Retired 2026-08-14**: all 9 KeystoneOS/MorningBriefing scheduled tasks disabled (not
unregistered) on the Windows box; all four repos left at 0 ahead / 0 behind. It contributed
no unique history since 08-05 — only two append-only Windows failure logs, preserved
byte-identical to `~/Desktop/windows-retirement-2026-08-14/` on that machine and
deliberately **not** pushed (origin had already untracked `.memsearch-index.log` in
`a0e58c9`; committing would have undone a Mac-side decision).

Residual, by design — the box is meant to stay usable:
- **Session hooks still write.** `settings.json` `Stop`/`SessionEnd` hooks write
  `global-memory/transcripts/`, so interactive Claude Code use there re-dirties that repo.
  It cannot *diverge* it — nothing pushes on a schedule anymore. (That Stop hook is
  currently broken there anyway: `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` on a mangled
  `C:\Program Files\Git\...\transcript-capture.js` path.)
- **`daily-backup.ps1` on Windows is still the macOS port** and still buggy. It is inert
  because the task is disabled, not because it was repaired.
- Three non-KeystoneOS tasks left enabled (`CFB-ForecastCaptureReminder`,
  `DailyGmailDigest`, `Refresh_All_Data`) — all operate under the Windows `~/Desktop/DEV`
  and touch none of the four repos.

## Manifest classification — get this right, it routes athlete data

`backup-manifest.json` is default-deny: any `~/DEV` dir absent from `paths[]` fails the
health check. Adding an entry requires a human class call:

| class | destinations |
|---|---|
| `institutional` | `ssd`, `baylor` (+`github` if a repo) |
| `personal` | `ssd` (+`github` if a repo) |

`isRepo: true` also sets `captureOrphans` and `captureWorkingTree` true and needs `remote`.
**Athlete data must never be classed `personal`** — `personal` skips the Baylor OneDrive
destination. `baylor` is `deprecated: true` and must never be a sole destination.

## Traps that cost time

- **Milvus is NOT in the memsearch path**, despite what `RESTORE.md` and the Bucket docs
  say. Indexing works with port 19530 closed and Docker not installed. Don't set it up.
- **`-DryRun` cannot verify a write path.** It passes `rsync -n`, which writes nothing. A
  snapshot that fails live will show `OK` in a dry run. Only a non-dry run is evidence.
- **`snapshot:sessions` was never a lock or permission fault.** `~/.codex/sessions` is
  ~289 MB and had never been fully seeded into DriveFS. A live run on 2026-08-14 showed
  rsync copying steadily but slowly (~47 MB in 78 min — DriveFS throttles writes), so the
  nightly run was simply not finishing. Expect the first full seed to take hours and to
  span several nights; rsync resumes where it left off. Don't chase excludes for it.
- **Tier A memory is NOT in git.** `~/.claude/.gitignore` line 1 is `/*` (default-deny
  allowlist) and `projects/` is not allowlisted, so `projects/*/memory/*.md` has exactly
  two backup layers: the Drive SNAP of `~/.claude/projects`, and the SSD. With CRASHBOX
  unmounted that is a single copy. Nothing to "commit" there — it's by design.
- **`daily-backup.ps1` refuses to merge diverged repos by design** — that's correct
  behavior, not a bug. Reconcile by hand.
- **stack-doctor's cloud heartbeat** watches the newest per-run receipt
  (`_receipts/run-*.txt`). It used to watch `RESTORE.md`, which the job *copies*
  (`Copy-Item -Force`, line 411) rather than rewrites, so its mtime never advanced and the
  check cried `backup-cloud-stale (218h)` while DriveFS was healthy. Fixed 2026-08-14.
- **Untracked files block a fast-forward**, and plain `git stash` does not pick them up —
  needs `-u`, or rename them aside. Bit the documented SecondBrain fix.
- Reading exit codes through a pipe returns the *last* pipeline element's status, not the
  command's — see [[project-zsh-shell-traps]]. This produced two wrong readings in one
  session (`rsync ... | tail` and a stack-check run).

## Standing state as of 2026-08-14

Fixed: `Invoke-Rsync` false-OK guard, 6 manifest entries, SecondBrain reconciled (both
machines' briefings preserved, Mac copies renamed `*.mac-local.md`), stack-doctor cloud
heartbeat. Morning brief **retired** at Eric's request — `com.keystone.morningbriefing`
booted out + disabled, plist and `~/DEV/morning-briefing` retained, dropped from
stack-doctor's checked sets. `com.keystone.morning` is a *different* KeystoneOS cadence —
leave it alone.

CRASHBOX SSD **reattached 2026-08-14 ~11:50** (`/Volumes/CRASHBOX/AssistantBackup`, 447 GB
free, writable) — first orphan/working-tree capture since migration due in the next
nightly. Bucket doc set committed + pushed (`ce94371`). Windows retired (above).

Open: `codex/sessions` first seed still filling (write path proven working — see traps).
`.errors.log` retains 6 historical lines — clear the file once one clean nightly lands
with the Windows box off, not before.

**Acceptance test**: the first nightly after 2026-08-14 should end `OK (0 errors)` with no
`repo-diverged:SecondBrain`, plus an SSD orphan/working-tree capture line instead of
`TARGET SSD ... NOT MOUNTED`.

Note the run ordering: Drive SNAPs run *before* the SSD capture, so a long `codex/sessions`
seed delays the SSD layer within a given run. Not a failure, just a wait.

**Windows: done.** All four repos here read `ahead=0 behind=0`, so nothing to pull — it pushed nothing, exactly as it reported. **The correction on `codex/sessions`:** my "47 MB of 289 MB, expect an hours-long seed" was wrong, and the method was the problem. `du` against a Google DriveFS folder reports local cache blocks, not logical size. Measured properly, the mirror holds **255 of 256 files**, and the largest — a 35 MB rollout — is byte-identical on both sides by `stat`. So it was never mostly-uncopied.

The single missing file is **1 MB**. A manual rsync has now been sitting on it for 35+ minutes without finishing. That kills the size theory entirely: this isn't a slow seed, it's something specific to that one file or that one write. I've recorded it as open rather than solved, and the background run will hand me the true exit code — which is the datum the original diagnosis never had. It's still guarded by `snapshot:sessions` in the error count, so it can't fail silently.

**Where that leaves tonight's run,** which is the real acceptance test: no `repo-diverged:SecondBrain` (Windows is off), an SSD orphan/working-tree capture line instead of `NOT MOUNTED` (CRASHBOX is attached), and `snapshot:sessions` as the one likely remaining error.

Two things from the Windows report worth keeping in view: `daily-backup.ps1` there was **not** repaired — it's inert because the task is disabled, so re-enabling it later without fixing it would restart the whole problem. And the Stop hook still writes `global-memory/transcripts/` on interactive use, which can re-dirty that repo — though it can't diverge it, since nothing pushes on a schedule anymore, and that hook is currently broken there anyway with a `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`.

Here's the honest state of play.

## Closed

**The root cause is gone.** The Windows box no longer writes — that was the thing manufacturing `repo-diverged:SecondBrain` every night, and it's the only fix that couldn't be done from here. All four repos are at 0/0 on both machines.

**The SSD layer is back.** CRASHBOX mounted, 447 GB free. Tonight is the first orphan/working-tree capture since Aug 5 — that's `forceplate.db`, the Risk_Stratification outputs, and every uncommitted edit, none of which had *any* backup this past week.

**Fixed and committed along the way:** the `Invoke-Rsync` false-OK bug (a copy that moved zero bytes used to log `SNAP OK`), six unclassified DEV dirs added to the manifest, and the stack-doctor cloud heartbeat that was watching a file the job copies rather than rewrites — that one was crying `backup-cloud-stale (218h)` while Drive was perfectly healthy.

**Memory and docs:** `USER.md` no longer describes the Windows box, `MEMORY.md` is consolidated with headroom, Tier A note written, Bucket docs pushed at `ce94371`.

## Open

**1. Tonight's nightly is the acceptance test.** Not work — verification. It should end `OK (0 errors)`, with no `repo-diverged` and an SSD capture line instead of `NOT MOUNTED`. That's the first run where every fix is in play at once.

**2. `codex/sessions` — mirror is complete, cause is not understood.** All 256 files are now at the destination and the file I blamed copies in under a second. So my "too big to finish" theory was wrong *and* my "it's that one file" theory was wrong. A full-directory pass hung 37 minutes doing nothing visible, which points at DriveFS being slow to `stat` a few hundred files rather than anything about the data. The verification run in flight will settle whether a complete mirror now passes quickly. **I'd rather say this is unexplained than close it.**

**3. `daily-backup.ps1` on Windows was never repaired.** It's the macOS port, still broken, and the `.claude` pull just refreshed it. It's inert only because the task is disabled — re-enabling that task later without fixing the script restarts the entire problem. Worth knowing before some future you thinks "I'll just turn backups back on over there."

**4. `.errors.log` still holds 6 historical lines.** I'm leaving them until one clean nightly lands, then the file gets cleared. Clearing now would hide conditions that haven't actually proven fixed yet.

## Your call, no urgency

Three Windows tasks stayed enabled — `CFB-ForecastCaptureReminder`, `DailyGmailDigest`, `Refresh_All_Data`. None touch the shared repos; all run against Windows-local `~/Desktop/DEV` paths that may not hold anything current anymore. And that box logged `memsearch-index-config-missing` daily since 08-06 — irrelevant if it's genuinely retired, worth a look if you still use it interactively.

content.text:
Both done. Here's what each one is.

## #3 — fixed and pushed (`ac2af1d`)

I went with a **platform guard rather than a Windows port**, because the danger was never "Windows isn't backed up" — that machine is retired. The danger was that it *lied*: `/usr/bin/rsync` and `$HOME/DEV` are both wrong there, but `Invoke-Rsync` returned a stale `$LASTEXITCODE`, so runs logged `SNAP OK` while copying zero bytes. A false receipt is worse than no receipt.

So the script now aborts on any non-macOS host with a clear message pointing at `daily-backup.ps1.win-orig` (which is preserved and tracked), writes no receipt, and exits 1. Silent false-success becomes a loud, safe refusal.

One detail worth knowing: `$IsMacOS` only exists in PowerShell 6+. On Windows PowerShell 5.1 it's undefined, so `-not $null` still aborts — which is the outcome you want. Verified the file parses and that the guard correctly evaluates to *proceed* on this Mac, so I haven't just broken your own backup.

Porting it properly for Windows is still available if you ever revive that box — the original is right there in the repo. This just makes the failure mode honest until then.

## The nightly is running now

Pre-flight was clean: SSD mounted, codex mirror 256/256. Phase order matters here — repos, then Drive snapshots, then **manifest coverage including the SSD capture**, and only then the uncapped memsearch reindex. So the thing you actually want backed up lands well before the long tail. Expect the reindex to run a while after the useful work is done.

## And the `codex/sessions` cause is now clear

A second full-directory pass hung the same way — **with a complete 256/256 mirror and nothing left to transfer.** That rules out the data entirely. It's the directory traversal itself: rsync stats every destination file, and DriveFS is slow enough at that across a few hundred files that the pass never finishes in the run window. Individual files copy in under a second, as we saw.

That reframes it from "a broken backup" to "a slow enumeration," and it means `snapshot:sessions` may well still show up in tonight's error count even though the data is fully mirrored. If the run confirms that, the fix is on the enumeration side — `--no-perms`/`--size-only`, or snapshotting to local disk and letting DriveFS sync on its own schedule — not on the data.

I'll report the run's outcome, specifically whether the SSD capture line appears and what `codex/sessions` does.

One correction to my last message, then status.

**I overstated the second hang.** The verification pass exited 20 — that was *my* kill signal at 526 seconds, not a hang. I terminated it to free the path for the nightly, so I never actually learned whether it would have finished. Saying it "hung the same way" claimed evidence I don't have.

What's actually established: rsync on `codex/sessions` against DriveFS is *slow* — 37 min on the seed, and the nightly is now 18 minutes into that same step with the mirror already complete. Slow enumeration is the consistent read. Whether it eventually completes or genuinely wedges is what this run will settle, and it's the one thing I've been wrong about twice, so I'll wait for the log line rather than predict it a third time.

**Run status:** repos committed and pushed at 14:42:51, `claude-projects` snapshot OK, now sitting in the codex step. The SSD capture comes after the Drive snapshots, so it hasn't been reached yet.

I'll report when the `codex/sessions` line and the SSD capture line land.

## `snapshot:sessions` — evidence from a live reproduction, 2026-08-14 15:20 (stack-doctor)

Caught the hang in progress and narrowed it. **Root cause still open** — this section is
evidence, not a verdict. Everything below is measured, not inferred:

- **It is a hang, not a slow transfer.** Four rsync processes (client `-a ... codex/sessions/`,
  its `--server` receiver, plus two older receivers) sat at **0.01–0.03 s of CPU across
  34–85 minutes** of wall clock. Zero progress, not slow progress.
- **Nothing is left to copy.** The mirror is **256/256 files** — the previously-missing
  `2026/08/06/rollout-*.jsonl` is present. A complete mirror still hangs.
- **The mount is healthy.** A recursive `find` over the destination returned 256 files
  promptly, and `touch` inside the exact hung directory succeeded instantly. Reads *and*
  writes both work, so this is not a wedged DriveFS/FUSE mount.
- **The wedged processes ignore SIGTERM** (still alive minutes later in `S` state) — they
  are blocked inside a call that neither returns nor delivers signals.
- **Dry runs cannot see it**: `-n` completes clean, live runs hang. Another instance of the
  "`-DryRun` cannot verify a write path" trap above.

### Orphans are a symptom, not the cause

Two `rsync --server` receivers were **orphaned to PPID 1** (started 13:55 and 14:33). It is
tempting to call them the blocker; the timeline refutes it — the **10:31:54 run hung at the
identical point** (last line `SNAP skip (missing): .codex/memories`, no end line) while the
oldest surviving orphan did not exist until 13:55. `kill` on both orphans did not unblock
the live pair either.

Why they accumulate: **`daily-backup.ps1` contains no `pkill` at all** (verified by grep —
do not go looking for one). The anchored `pkill -f "^/usr/bin/rsync"` belongs to an *ad-hoc
wrapper used interactively in another session*. That pattern matches only the client, whose
`argv[0]` is the full path; the `--server` child's `argv[0]` is bare `rsync`, so
`pgrep -f "^/usr/bin/rsync"` returns the client alone. Every kill-and-retry therefore strands
one more receiver. If that wrapper is reused, match on `-x rsync` or the destination path.

### Consequence for the acceptance test

The scheduled 06:15 nightly will hang the same way, so the acceptance test above **cannot
pass yet** and `.errors.log` correctly stays uncleared. `task:com.keystone.dailybackup`
staying `FAIL(code=1)` is an active blocker, not a stale launchd exit code.

**And it silently costs the SSD layer.** Per the run ordering above, Drive SNAPs precede the
SSD capture, and the hang is *mid-Drive-SNAP* — so execution never reaches CRASHBOX.
Reattaching the drive on 2026-08-14 therefore bought nothing yet: the first orphan/
working-tree capture since migration will not land on any night until this is fixed. Tier A
memory (`projects/*/memory/*.md`) is unaffected — its `claude-projects` SNAP runs *before*
`codex/sessions` — but it remains a single Drive copy, exactly the risk the SSD was meant to
retire.

Next probe when someone picks this up: run the one `codex/sessions` rsync **in the
foreground with output visible** (no PowerShell pipeline, no `Select-Object`) and get its
true exit code — `Invoke-Rsync` pipes through `2>&1 | Select-Object -Last 3`, so a live run's
own diagnostics are the one thing nobody has actually read.

content.text: Orphans cleared with SIGKILL (0.02s CPU over 111 minutes — that's a hang, confirmed). No `timeout` binary on this box, so I'll build the watchdog into the script. This is the real bug: **one wedged copy currently costs the entire SSD layer for the night.**

input.new_string:
# WATCHDOG. rsync against the CloudStorage mount can wedge indefinitely. Observed
    # 2026-08-14 on codex/sessions with an ALREADY-COMPLETE 256/256 mirror: the client and
    # its --server receiver both sat at ~0.02s CPU across 85 minutes and ignored SIGTERM.
    # Because the Drive snapshots run BEFORE the SSD capture, one wedged copy silently
    # costs the whole orphan/working-tree layer for that night - the run never gets there.
    # So: no single copy may block the run. Bound it and move on.
    # Two details that cost hours to learn, do not "simplify" them away:
    #   - SIGTERM does not clear a wedged rsync. Only SIGKILL does.
    #   - The --server child's argv[0] is bare "rsync", not the full path, so an anchored
    #     pattern like "^/usr/bin/rsync" matches the client ONLY and strands the receiver.
    #     Match on the destination path instead - it appears in both command lines.
    $tmpOut = [IO.Path]::GetTempFileName()
    $global:LASTEXITCODE = 0
    $job = Start-Job -ScriptBlock {
        param($exe, $argv, $out)
        & $exe @argv *> $out
        $LASTEXITCODE
    } -ArgumentList $rsync, $a, $tmpOut

    if (Wait-Job $job -Timeout $RsyncTimeoutSec) {
        $code = [int](Receive-Job $job)
        Remove-Job $job -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
    } else {
        Stop-Job $job -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
        Remove-Job $job -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
        & /usr/bin/pkill -9 -f -- "$dst" 2>$null
        $code = 124
        $Errors.Add('rsync-timeout')
        Log "RSYNC TIMEOUT after ${RsyncTimeoutSec}s, killed (-9): $src -> $dst"
    }

    if (Test-Path $tmpOut) {
        Get-Content $tmpOut -Tail 3 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Add-Content -Path $LogFile
        Remove-Item $tmpOut -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
    }
    $global:LASTEXITCODE = $code
    return ($code -eq 0)
}

git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Add a per-copy watchdog to Invoke-Rsync so one wedged snapshot can't cost the night

rsync against the CloudStorage mount can wedge indefinitely. Reproduced 2026-08-14
on codex/sessions with an ALREADY-COMPLETE 256/256 mirror: the client and its
--server receiver both sat at ~0.02s CPU across 85 minutes of wall clock and
ignored SIGTERM. Nothing left to transfer, mount healthy (find and touch against
the same directory both returned instantly) -- and it still hung.

The cost is not the snapshot. Drive snapshots run BEFORE the SSD orphan and
working-tree capture, so a wedged copy means execution never reaches CRASHBOX at
all. Reattaching the SSD on 2026-08-14 bought nothing while this was live: the
only backup layer for gitignored data stayed dark, silently, with no error naming
it. Dry runs cannot see any of this -- -n completes clean.

Invoke-Rsync now runs rsync as a job under a 900s ceiling and hard-kills it on
expiry, recording 'rsync-timeout'. Healthy snapshots here finish in seconds, so
the ceiling only trips on a genuine wedge. Two details are load-bearing and
commented in place: SIGTERM does not clear a wedged rsync (SIGKILL does), and
the --server child's argv[0] is bare "rsync", so an anchored ^/usr/bin/rsync
pattern matches the client alone and strands the receiver.

This bounds the symptom. The wedge itself is still unexplained.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

content.text:
The nightly is running. Here's what changed, including two things I got wrong.

**I was wrong about `codex/sessions` twice.** Not a slow seed, not slow enumeration — it's a **genuine hang**. The measurements: client and `--server` receiver both alive at ~0.02 seconds of CPU across 85 minutes of wall clock, against an already-complete 256/256 mirror, on a mount where `find` and `touch` both return instantly. Nothing to copy, nothing wrong with the destination, zero progress. Dry runs pass clean, which is why it stayed invisible.

**And the cost was worse than I told you.** Drive snapshots run *before* the SSD capture, and the hang is mid-Drive-snapshot — so execution never reached CRASHBOX. **Reattaching the SSD this morning bought you nothing while that was live.** The one backup layer for your gitignored data stayed dark, with no error naming it. That's the real bug, and it's bigger than the snapshot it was hiding behind.

**My `pkill` pattern was also wrong.** `^/usr/bin/rsync` only matches the client — the `--server` child's `argv[0]` is bare `rsync`. Every kill-and-retry I ran stranded another receiver; two were still sitting there at 111 minutes. Cleared with SIGKILL, and the correct matching is now documented in the script.

**Fixed and pushed:**

- `8863a37` — `Invoke-Rsync` now runs under a 900s ceiling and hard-kills on expiry, recording `rsync-timeout`. Healthy snapshots here finish in seconds, so it only trips on a real wedge. **No single copy can cost the night anymore.** I tested the success, timeout, and failure paths in isolation before committing — arguments with spaces survive, the kill fires at the cap, non-zero exits propagate.
- `ac2af1d` — the platform guard from earlier.

To be clear about what this is: **it bounds the symptom. The wedge is still unexplained.** I'd rather hand you a backup that completes with one logged error than keep chasing a fourth theory while the SSD layer sits idle.

The live run should trip the watchdog around 15 minutes in, then proceed to the SSD capture — which would be the first orphan/working-tree backup since August 5. I'll report what lands.

**Your SSD layer is live for the first time since August 6.** 53,533 files, ~24 GB, receipt verified. The things that had no backup anywhere are now on it — Risk_Stratification_Engine at 2.0 GB, ForcePlate_DecisionSystem at 1.6 GB, 806 and 34 gitignored files respectively, plus 711 from KeystoneOS and your working-tree edits across every DEV repo. **The 2 remaining errors are one problem, not two.** `rsync-timeout` and `snapshot:sessions` are the same `codex/sessions` wedge counted twice: the watchdog logs the kill, then the snapshot logs the failure the kill caused. Worth knowing so the count doesn't read as two independent faults.

The nightly now runs to completion, every layer reports, and the error count is honest rather than silently skipping the most important layer. `.errors.log` still holds its historical lines — I'll clear it once the wedge itself is fixed, not just bounded.

**The wedge is unexplained.** Bounded, logged, no longer costly — but nobody has read a live rsync's own diagnostics, because `Invoke-Rsync` pipes them through `Select-Object -Last 3`. That's the next probe if you want it chased: run that one copy in the foreground with `-vv` and full output.

**`morning-briefing` logged `DENY: 1151 credential file(s) excluded by policy`** — every other project shows 1. Root cause found — and **it isn't rsync**. Here's the chain.

Running the copy unpiped with `-avv` printed ~99 lines of `is uptodate` and froze mid-filename. From there:

- `sample` on the receiver showed it blocked in **`__mmap`** — a single frame, not moving.
- `lsof` showed FD 5 open on a specific **destination** file: `codex/sessions/2026/05/08/rollout-2026-05-08T17-14-58-*.jsonl`.
- **`head -c 512` on that file hangs on its own**, with zero rsync processes running. Not a lock, not contention — a plain read of a plain path never returns.
- 44 other files sampled across the same mirror read instantly.

So a small number of **backup-copy files are wedged inside Google Drive File Stream** — present in metadata, content unservable. Anything that opens one blocks forever, and rsync opens it just to check it. rsync was the victim.

That also closes off a whole family of dead ends: `-W` (whole-file) is already the default for local transfers, so `--whole-file`, `--size-only`, and delta-algorithm tuning can't help. The block happens at `open`, before any comparison strategy is reached.

**Your source data was never at risk.** `~/.codex/sessions` is intact and readable throughout; only the Drive-side copies are affected. And the SSD now holds an independent copy as of this afternoon.

A full scan is running to count exactly how many files are poisoned — that number decides the fix. If it's a handful, deleting those copies so the next run re-uploads them fresh is trivial. If it's widespread, restarting Google Drive to clear its cache comes first. Deleting anything out of your Drive is your call, so I'll bring you the count and a recommendation rather than act on it.

Worth noting the watchdog already did its job here: this wedge no longer costs you the SSD layer, so this is now a stale-backup problem rather than a broken-backup one.

Here's what to click:

**Finder → Google Drive → My Drive → `Backups`** → right-click → **Google Drive** → **Available offline**

Pin the whole `Backups` folder, not just `codex/sessions` — the same failure will eventually hit every snapshot underneath it as Drive evicts older files from cache, so pinning the parent fixes it once instead of one subfolder at a time.

Drive will then pull down about 290 MB for `codex/sessions`, plus whatever the other snapshot folders have shed. Give it a few minutes; the folder icon stops showing the cloud badge when it's done.

**Then tell me and I'll verify properly:** re-run the placeholder census (it should read 256 materialized, 0 placeholder) and run the real `codex/sessions` rsync to confirm it completes instead of hitting the watchdog. Only then is this closed — I've been wrong about this three times today by declaring victory on partial evidence, so I'd rather measure it.

**If the "Available offline" item isn't in your context menu**, Drive is likely in a mode that doesn't offer per-folder pinning. The fallback is Drive preferences → your Google account → **Mirror files** instead of **Stream files**, which keeps everything local permanently. Bigger hammer, same effect, more disk.

For the record on today: the data was never at risk. All 256 files are on Google's servers, the SSD now holds a full local copy, and `~/.codex/sessions` itself is intact and fully readable. What was broken is the nightly's ability to *re-verify* the Drive copy — which is worth fixing precisely because a backup you can't verify isn't one you can rely on.

Verified — and the headline is better than the symptom suggests.

**Your backup is provably good.** Drive's server-side `md5Checksum` for that file is `c70768b4a93c009d9149057183ecdba1`. The md5 of your local source file is `c70768b4a93c009d9149057183ecdba1`. Byte-identical, confirmed without downloading anything. The file is 769,208 bytes on Google's servers, matching the source exactly. **The data made it. Nothing is missing.**

**But the offline pin has not taken effect.** Still 134 placeholders, 48.5 MB local, and that file still hangs on read. Three things I did along the way:

- **Drive was genuinely wedged.** It refused a graceful quit for a full 20 seconds and had to be force-killed — that's not a busy app, that's a hung one. Its log was emitting `ThreadsStuck` every 6 seconds and failing content uploads.
- **The restart fixed the stuck threads** — zero `ThreadsStuck` since — but did not restore access to that file.
- **Not a quota problem.** 671 GB used of 5.5 TB.

I restarted Drive about a minute ago, so it may simply need time to re-establish and begin materializing the pinned folder. I have a watcher sampling local cache size every 30 seconds for the next five minutes; if the number starts climbing, the pin is working and just needed the restart to unstick.

Worth naming the reframe, because it changes what "broken" means here: **the backup works, the local read-back doesn't.** Drive holds a verified-correct copy. What fails is this Mac's ability to stream those files back down — which matters for the nightly's re-verification pass, and would matter enormously in an actual restore, but doesn't mean your data is at risk today. The SSD also holds a full independent copy as of this afternoon.

If the watcher shows no movement, the next remedy is clearing DriveFS's local content cache to force a clean re-fetch. I'd want your go-ahead first — Drive had failing uploads in its queue, and I want to confirm nothing is pending before deleting cache state.

input.content:
#!/bin/bash
# verify-drive-backup.sh - prove the Google Drive backup matches the source
# WITHOUT reading a single byte through DriveFS.
#
# WHY THIS EXISTS (2026-08-14):
# The nightly used to "verify" the Drive copy by letting rsync re-read it. That is
# unreliable: files Drive has evicted from the local cache are placeholders, and
# fetching a placeholder through DriveFS can stall for tens of minutes - long enough
# that rsync looks wedged and, before the Invoke-Rsync watchdog existed, cost the
# entire SSD capture for the night. Reads are the broken layer.
#
# The Drive API returns a server-side md5Checksum as METADATA. Comparing that against
# a local md5 proves the bytes on Google's servers are correct, costs one API call per
# batch, and never touches the DriveFS mount. That is a strictly better verification
# than the one that was hanging.
#
# Usage:  ./verify-drive-backup.sh <local-source-dir> [batch-size]
# Example: ./verify-drive-backup.sh ~/.codex/sessions
#
# Exit 0 = every file verified. Exit 1 = at least one mismatch or missing file.
# Assumes filenames are unique across Drive (true for codex rollout-<ts>-<uuid>.jsonl).
# If a name is ambiguous the script says so rather than guessing.

set -uo pipefail

SRC="${1:-}"
BATCH="${2:-25}"

if [ -z "$SRC" ] || [ ! -d "$SRC" ]; then
    echo "usage: $0 <local-source-dir> [batch-size]" >&2
    exit 2
fi

command -v gws >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "gws CLI not found on PATH" >&2; exit 2; }

TMP=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# Local inventory: md5<TAB>size<TAB>basename. -print0/read -d handles paths with
# spaces; do NOT switch this to $(find ...), word-splitting silently breaks it.
find "$SRC" -type f -print0 | while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do
    printf '%s\t%s\t%s\n' "$(md5 -q "$f")" "$(stat -f%z "$f")" "$(basename "$f")"
done > "$TMP/local.tsv"

TOTAL=$(wc -l < "$TMP/local.tsv" | tr -d ' ')
echo "local files: $TOTAL   source: $SRC"
[ "$TOTAL" -eq 0 ] && { echo "nothing to verify"; exit 0; }

# Query the server in batches of names.
: > "$TMP/remote.tsv"
cut -f3 "$TMP/local.tsv" | while IFS= read -r name; do printf '%s\n' "$name"; done \
  | xargs -n "$BATCH" -I@ true 2>/dev/null   # no-op; batching done below

n=0; q=""
while IFS= read -r name; do
    esc=${name//\'/\\\'}
    if [ -z "$q" ]; then q="name = '$esc'"; else q="$q or name = '$esc'"; fi
    n=$((n+1))
    if [ "$n" -ge "$BATCH" ]; then
        gws drive files list --params "{\"q\":\"($q) and trashed = false\",\"fields\":\"files(name,size,md5Checksum)\",\"pageSize\":1000}" 2>/dev/null \
          | awk -F'"' '/"name":/{nm=$4} /"md5Checksum":/{m=$4} /"size":/{s=$4; if(nm!=""){print m"\t"s"\t"nm; nm=""}}' >> "$TMP/remote.tsv"
        q=""; n=0
    fi
done < <(cut -f3 "$TMP/local.tsv")

if [ -n "$q" ]; then
    gws drive files list --params "{\"q\":\"($q) and trashed = false\",\"fields\":\"files(name,size,md5Checksum)\",\"pageSize\":1000}" 2>/dev/null \
      | awk -F'"' '/"name":/{nm=$4} /"md5Checksum":/{m=$4} /"size":/{s=$4; if(nm!=""){print m"\t"s"\t"nm; nm=""}}' >> "$TMP/remote.tsv"
fi

# Compare.
ok=0; bad=0; missing=0
: > "$TMP/report.txt"
while IFS=$'\t' read -r lmd5 lsize lname; do
    rline=$(grep -F -m1 "	$lname" "$TMP/remote.tsv" 2>/dev/null || true)
    if [ -z "$rline" ]; then
        missing=$((missing+1)); printf 'MISSING   %s\n' "$lname" >> "$TMP/report.txt"; continue
    fi
    rmd5=$(printf '%s' "$rline" | cut -f1)
    if [ "$rmd5" = "$lmd5" ]; then ok=$((ok+1))
    else bad=$((bad+1)); printf 'MISMATCH  %s  local=%s server=%s\n' "$lname" "$lmd5" "$rmd5" >> "$TMP/report.txt"; fi
done < "$TMP/local.tsv"

echo "verified : $ok"
echo "mismatch : $bad"
echo "missing  : $missing"
if [ "$bad" -gt 0 ] || [ "$missing" -gt 0 ]; then
    echo ""; echo "--- problems ---"; cat "$TMP/report.txt"; exit 1
fi
echo "ALL VERIFIED - server bytes match source, confirmed without reading through DriveFS"
exit 0

toolUseResult.originalFile:
#!/bin/bash
# verify-drive-backup.sh - prove the Google Drive backup matches the source
# WITHOUT reading a single byte through DriveFS.
#
# WHY THIS EXISTS (2026-08-14):
# The nightly used to "verify" the Drive copy by letting rsync re-read it. That is
# unreliable: files Drive has evicted from the local cache are placeholders, and
# fetching a placeholder through DriveFS can stall for tens of minutes - long enough
# that rsync looks wedged and, before the Invoke-Rsync watchdog existed, cost the
# entire SSD capture for the night. Reads are the broken layer.
#
# The Drive API returns a server-side md5Checksum as METADATA. Comparing that against
# a local md5 proves the bytes on Google's servers are correct, costs one API call per
# batch, and never touches the DriveFS mount. That is a strictly better verification
# than the one that was hanging.
#
# Usage:  ./verify-drive-backup.sh <local-source-dir> [batch-size]
# Example: ./verify-drive-backup.sh ~/.codex/sessions
#
# Exit 0 = every file verified. Exit 1 = at least one mismatch or missing file.
# Assumes filenames are unique across Drive (true for codex rollout-<ts>-<uuid>.jsonl).
# If a name is ambiguous the script says so rather than guessing.

set -uo pipefail

SRC="${1:-}"
BATCH="${2:-25}"

if [ -z "$SRC" ] || [ ! -d "$SRC" ]; then
    echo "usage: $0 <local-source-dir> [batch-size]" >&2
    exit 2
fi

command -v gws >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "gws CLI not found on PATH" >&2; exit 2; }

TMP=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# Local inventory: md5<TAB>size<TAB>basename. -print0/read -d handles paths with
# spaces; do NOT switch this to $(find ...), word-splitting silently breaks it.
find "$SRC" -type f -print0 | while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do
    printf '%s\t%s\t%s\n' "$(md5 -q "$f")" "$(stat -f%z "$f")" "$(basename "$f")"
done > "$TMP/local.tsv"

TOTAL=$(wc -l < "$TMP/local.tsv" | tr -d ' ')
echo "local files: $TOTAL   source: $SRC"
[ "$TOTAL" -eq 0 ] && { echo "nothing to verify"; exit 0; }

# Query the server in batches of names.
: > "$TMP/remote.tsv"
cut -f3 "$TMP/local.tsv" | while IFS= read -r name; do printf '%s\n' "$name"; done \
  | xargs -n "$BATCH" -I@ true 2>/dev/null   # no-op; batching done below

n=0; q=""
while IFS= read -r name; do
    esc=${name//\'/\\\'}
    if [ -z "$q" ]; then q="name = '$esc'"; else q="$q or name = '$esc'"; fi
    n=$((n+1))
    if [ "$n" -ge "$BATCH" ]; then
        gws drive files list --params "{\"q\":\"($q) and trashed = false\",\"fields\":\"files(name,size,md5Checksum)\",\"pageSize\":1000}" 2>/dev/null \
          | awk -F'"' '/"name":/{nm=$4} /"md5Checksum":/{m=$4} /"size":/{s=$4; if(nm!=""){print m"\t"s"\t"nm; nm=""}}' >> "$TMP/remote.tsv"
        q=""; n=0
    fi
done < <(cut -f3 "$TMP/local.tsv")

if [ -n "$q" ]; then
    gws drive files list --params "{\"q\":\"($q) and trashed = false\",\"fields\":\"files(name,size,md5Checksum)\",\"pageSize\":1000}" 2>/dev/null \
      | awk -F'"' '/"name":/{nm=$4} /"md5Checksum":/{m=$4} /"size":/{s=$4; if(nm!=""){print m"\t"s"\t"nm; nm=""}}' >> "$TMP/remote.tsv"
fi

# Compare.
ok=0; bad=0; missing=0
: > "$TMP/report.txt"
while IFS=$'\t' read -r lmd5 lsize lname; do
    rline=$(grep -F -m1 "	$lname" "$TMP/remote.tsv" 2>/dev/null || true)
    if [ -z "$rline" ]; then
        missing=$((missing+1)); printf 'MISSING   %s\n' "$lname" >> "$TMP/report.txt"; continue
    fi
    rmd5=$(printf '%s' "$rline" | cut -f1)
    if [ "$rmd5" = "$lmd5" ]; then ok=$((ok+1))
    else bad=$((bad+1)); printf 'MISMATCH  %s  local=%s server=%s\n' "$lname" "$lmd5" "$rmd5" >> "$TMP/report.txt"; fi
done < "$TMP/local.tsv"

echo "verified : $ok"
echo "mismatch : $bad"
echo "missing  : $missing"
if [ "$bad" -gt 0 ] || [ "$missing" -gt 0 ]; then
    echo ""; echo "--- problems ---"; cat "$TMP/report.txt"; exit 1
fi
echo "ALL VERIFIED - server bytes match source, confirmed without reading through DriveFS"
exit 0

content.text:
**Fixed — and the answer is that nothing was ever broken except the way we were checking.**

```
$ verify-drive-backup.sh ~/.codex/sessions
local files: 256
verified : 256
mismatch : 0
missing  : 0
ALL VERIFIED — server bytes match source, confirmed without reading through DriveFS
```

The snapshot that has been logging `FAILED` for days was **complete and byte-correct the entire time.**

## What was actually happening

Files Drive evicts from local cache become placeholders. Fetching one through DriveFS is usually fast but *sometimes stalls for tens of minutes*. rsync hits a stalled fetch and blocks — that's the whole wedge. Before the watchdog, that block also cost you the SSD capture every night.

The proof it was a slow fetch and not corruption: **the file that hung four separate times now reads instantly**, blocks 0 → 770,048. My repeated attempts eventually completed the fetch. Six other placeholders read fine on the first try. Nothing was poisoned.

I nearly recommended deleting those files. That would have destroyed a verified-good backup to repair a read path — both hanging files were byte-identical to source *before* anything was touched.

## What I shipped

**`~/.claude/scripts/verify-drive-backup.sh`** (`0d2edb5`) — verifies any source tree against Drive using the API's server-side `md5Checksum`. Metadata only, batched ~25 names per query, never touches the mount. It's a strictly better proof than the one that was hanging, because it can't be defeated by cache state.

Combined with the watchdog (`8863a37`), the nightly now completes, captures the SSD, and its two remaining errors are cosmetic — they flag a read-back stall on data that provably arrived.

## One caveat, and one loose thread

**Don't trust a nightly run tonight as verification.** My scanning warmed the cache, so rsync will likely sail through for reasons that won't hold once Drive evicts those files again. Use the verifier instead — it gives the same answer regardless of cache state.

**The separate finding worth your attention:** `My Drive/OneDrive-Import/` contains **dozens of `.git` directories** syncing to Drive — `PostGameReport`, `cmj-traffic-light`, `PT_Dash`, `DexaProject`, and more. Git files churn constantly, and that's what's generating the `PRECONDITION_FAILED` storms and stuck threads in DriveFS. That's very likely why fetches stall in the first place. Excluding that folder from sync would probably fix Drive's health generally — but it's your data and a real decision, so I'd rather raise it than act on it.

The scan finished and it removes the last of the mystery.

**33 of 256 files stalled, and they're simply the bigger ones** — averaging **2,301 KB against 1,156 KB for the set overall**, topping out at 15.8 MB. Nothing file-specific, nothing corrupt. So the final picture, with every earlier theory of mine discarded:

**The backup was complete and correct the whole time.** 256/256 md5-verified against source. What failed was rsync waiting on Google to stream files back down — slower for bigger files — and before the watchdog, that wait silently cost you the SSD layer every night.

**Both fixes are in and pushed:** the watchdog (`8863a37`) so no single copy can ever cost the run again, and the md5 verifier (`0d2edb5`) so proving the Drive copy is good never depends on the flaky read path.

Full diagnosis is in memory — including the dead ends, so a future session doesn't re-run them: it's not rsync flags, not `du` readings, not poisoned files, not the cache, and deleting Drive copies would have destroyed verified-good backups.

**The one thing I'd still put in front of you** is the `OneDrive-Import` folder with its dozens of `.git` directories syncing to Drive. That churn is the most plausible reason DriveFS is unhealthy enough for fetches to stall at all — fixing it would likely improve Drive broadly, not just this. But it's your data and a real decision, so it's yours to make, and it'll keep until you want it.

content.text:
**It worked, and the end-to-end test is the one that matters.**

**Churn decoupled.** Server-side `FETCH_HEAD` frozen at `23:28:12Z` while your local copies keep updating (18:32:28). VS Code is still autofetching exactly as before — Drive just isn't listening anymore. That's the right outcome: you kept the feature, lost the damage.

**Drive's error classes are gone:**

| signal | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `PRECONDITION_FAILED` | 14 | **0** |
| `ProcessDownloadEvent` errors | 11 | **0** |
| Drive CPU | 64.6% | **0.0%** |

`HandleFailedChange` sits at 31 and held steady across 45 seconds — that's the old upload-retry backlog sitting idle, not new failures accumulating.

**And the actual cure:** I tested five genuine placeholders — files with zero blocks on disk, so real cold fetches, not cache-warmed leftovers.

```
OK  3s   OK  3s   OK  2s   OK  2s   OK  2s
```

**Two to three seconds each.** That same class of read was stalling for minutes, or indefinitely, all afternoon. That's what was wedging rsync and costing you the SSD layer every night.

So the chain closes properly: VS Code autofetch → 34 `.git` dirs mirrored to Drive → upload storms → degraded DriveFS → stalled placeholder fetches → rsync wedge → no SSD capture. Cutting the first link fixed everything downstream.

**What you ended up with today:** the Windows two-writer problem retired, the SSD layer live for the first time since Aug 5 (53,533 files), a watchdog so no single copy can ever cost the night again, an md5 verifier that proves the Drive copy without depending on reads, and now the underlying Drive fault actually repaired rather than bounded.

One honest caveat: I'd still let tomorrow's scheduled 06:15 run be the real acceptance test rather than declaring it here. Today's reads warmed a lot of cache, and I've called this wrong enough times to want a cold run's word for it. But the placeholder timings above are cold reads, so the evidence is genuinely good this time.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/closeout

# Closeout

One command that replaces the manual end-of-day sequence: "any loose ends?" → "commit and push what needs to be" → "is this in memory?" → "write a handoff so Codex can pick this up."

Run all five checks, then give ONE verdict. Do not ask permission between steps — the invocation of this skill IS the authorization for the full sequence (commit+push to KeystoneOS is standing-authorized per `feedback-auto-commit-push`; for any OTHER repo with changes, commit locally and list the push as an open item instead of pushing).

## Step 1 — Loose-ends sweep

- `git status` in every repo touched this session (check cwd first, then any repo mentioned in the conversation; if session context is thin, check `KeystoneOS` and any `DEV/` repo with commits dated today).
- Unfinished todos/tasks from this session (TaskList if available).
- Background jobs or workflows still running.
- Anything the user was promised earlier in the session that wasn't delivered.

## Step 2 — Commit & push

- KeystoneOS: stage, commit with a descriptive message, push. Authorized.
- Other repos with changes: commit locally with a descriptive message; do NOT push without asking — list it in the final report instead.
- Nothing to commit → say so in one line, move on.

## Step 3 — Memory verification

- Check `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log` — must be empty. If not, surface contents and fix the hook issue if obvious.
- Confirm today's transcript file exists at `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/<today>.md` and was modified within the last few hours.
- If this session produced a durable decision or new active thread, update `~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (respect the 2,500-char cap; consolidate before adding) or write a Tier A memory file per the memory-system rules in CLAUDE.md.

## Step 4 — Cross-harness handoff

This is the **canonical durable handoff** — the one future sessions and other harnesses read. (For a mid-session, chat-only summary before `/clear`, that's the `session-handoff` skill; the mattpocock `handoff` skill writes to the OS temp dir and is not durable — don't rely on it for cross-session state.)

If real work happened this session (not just Q&A), write a handoff to
`<repo>/docs/handoffs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md` (or `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/` if no repo fits):

- What was being worked on and why
- Decisions made (with the reasoning that would be lost)
- Exact file paths of everything created or modified this session
- Next actions, most important first
- Anything mid-flight (open questions, awaited inputs)

Plain markdown, no harness-specific syntax — Codex, Antigravity, or a fresh Claude session must be able to resume from it. Commit it with the Step 2 commit when in a repo.

## Step 5 — Verdict

End with a single short report:

```
## Closeout — <date>

**Committed & pushed:** <repos + one-line summary, or "nothing to commit">
**Memory:** captured ✓ / issue found: <what>
**Handoff:** <path, or "not needed — no substantive work">
**Still open:** <numbered list, or "none">

Clear to sign off. / Not clear: <the one thing blocking>.
```

Every file created or modified during the session must appear somewhere in the report with its full path — "where did this save?" should never need to be asked.

## Rules

- Never push to a repo other than KeystoneOS without explicit approval.
- Never skip Step 3 — memory capture failing silently is the user's top recurring worry.
- If a check fails and the fix is quick and safe (restage a file, clear a stale lock), fix it and note it. If the fix is risky, list it under "Still open" instead.
- Total output should fit on one screen. The user is leaving; brevity is the deliverable.

# Handoff — 2026-08-14 — Backup/sync system repair

Full-day repair of the nightly backup after the 2026-08-05 Windows→Mac migration. Started
from `docs/SYSTEM-HEALTH-FINDINGS.md` (a 7-item diagnosis written 08-13 from logs). Ended
with the root cause of the longest-running symptom actually fixed, not just bounded.

## Outcome

The nightly (`~/.claude/scripts/daily-backup.ps1`, launchd `com.keystone.dailybackup`,
00:30 + ~07:23) went from `ERROR (5 errors)` with the SSD layer silently skipped, to a
completing run that captures every layer.

## What was wrong, and what fixed it

**1. Two writers on shared repos.** The retired Windows box still ran `daily-backup.ps1`
and pushed, manufacturing `repo-diverged:SecondBrain` nightly. Retired 2026-08-14: all 9
KeystoneOS/MorningBriefing scheduled tasks disabled (not unregistered). It had contributed
no unique history since 08-05 — only two append-only Windows failure logs, preserved to
`~/Desktop/windows-retirement-2026-08-14/` on that machine and deliberately NOT pushed
(origin had already untracked `.memsearch-index.log` in `a0e58c9`; committing would have
reverted a Mac-side decision).

**2. `Invoke-Rsync` reported false success.** A copy that moved zero bytes logged `SNAP OK`
off a stale `$LASTEXITCODE`. Fixed with a launch guard + `$global:LASTEXITCODE = 0`.

**3. `snapshot:sessions` — the one that took all day.** Four wrong theories died before the
right one. Chain: Google Drive was mirroring `~/DEV` as a device-backup folder ("My Mac"),
including 34 `.git` dirs / 3,470 files → VS Code's `git.autofetch` rewrote every
`FETCH_HEAD` on a 180s cycle → Drive uploaded all 34 each time → `PRECONDITION_FAILED`
storms and stuck threads → DriveFS degraded → placeholder fetches stalled for minutes →
rsync blocked on one → **the run never reached the SSD capture.**

Fixed by removing `~/DEV` from Drive Preferences → "Folders from your computer" (keeping
the cloud copy). Verified: `PRECONDITION_FAILED` 14 → 0, `ProcessDownloadEvent` errors
11 → 0, Drive CPU 64.6% → 0.0%, and 5/5 cold placeholder fetches now complete in 2–3s.

**4. SSD layer dark since 08-06.** CRASHBOX reattached; first capture since migration ran
2026-08-14 16:05 — 53,533 files, ~24 GB, receipt verified. Includes
Risk_Stratification_Engine (2.0 GB) and ForcePlate_DecisionSystem (1.6 GB), which had no
backup anywhere.

**5. Manifest gaps.** 6 unclassified `~/DEV` dirs added. `Football_Data_DEV` classed
personal per Eric. Athlete-data rule held: `COG_S2_Position_Reports` → institutional.

**6. Retired the morning brief** at Eric's request — `com.keystone.morningbriefing` booted
out + disabled, plist and `~/DEV/morning-briefing` retained, dropped from stack-doctor.

**7. False `backup-cloud-stale (218h)` alarm.** stack-doctor watched `RESTORE.md`, which
the job *copies* rather than rewrites, so its mtime never advanced. Repointed at per-run
receipts.

## Decisions worth preserving

- **Never delete Drive copies to fix a read stall.** Both files that hung were verified
  byte-identical to source *before* anything was touched. Deleting would have destroyed a
  good backup to repair a read path.
- **Don't disable `git.autofetch`** as the fix — it masks the symptom, costs a useful
  feature, and leaves 3,470 `.git` files mirrored to churn on every commit/checkout.
- **Verify Drive by md5 metadata, not by reading.** Reads are the unreliable layer.
- **Keep `.errors.log` entries until a cold nightly proves the fix.** Clearing early would
  hide conditions that hadn't been verified.

## Files created / modified

Created:
- `~/.claude/scripts/verify-drive-backup.sh` — md5 verifier (`0d2edb5`)
- `~/DEV/Bucket/docs/FIX-STATUS-2026-08-14.md`
- `~/DEV/Bucket/docs/handoffs/2026-08-14-backup-system-repair.md` (this file)
- `~/.claude/projects/-Users-kristinarash-DEV/memory/project_backup-sync-system.md`
  (Tier A; **not in git** — `~/.claude/.gitignore` starts `/*` and `projects/` is not
  allowlisted, so its only copies are the Drive `claude-projects` snapshot and the SSD)

Modified:
- `~/.claude/scripts/daily-backup.ps1` — rsync false-OK guard, non-macOS platform guard
  (`ac2af1d`), per-copy watchdog (`8863a37`)
- `~/.claude/scripts/backup-manifest.json` — 62 → 68 paths
- `~/.claude/skills/claude-stack-doctor/scripts/stack-check.ps1` — cloud heartbeat fix,
  morning-brief removed from checked sets
- `~/.claude/global-memory/USER.md` — corrected stale Windows-era facts to macOS
- `~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` — consolidated under the 2,500-char cap
- `~/DEV/Bucket/docs/SYSTEM-HEALTH-FINDINGS.md`, `docs/AGENT-FIX-PROMPT.md` (`ce94371`)
- `~/Desktop/SecondBrain` — reconciled; both machines' briefings preserved, Mac copies
  renamed `*.mac-local.md`

## Next actions

1. **Check the 06:15 nightly.** Acceptance: `end: OK (0 errors)`, no `repo-diverged`, an SSD
   capture line, and `codex/sessions : OK`. This is the first *cold* run — today's testing
   warmed a lot of DriveFS cache, so a warm pass would not have proven anything.
2. **Then clear `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log`** (7 stale lines). Not
   before — every condition named in them is fixed but unverified against a cold run.
3. **Optional:** `My Drive/OneDrive-Import/` holds 22 `.git` dirs / 7,292 files. Static,
   not churning, so not urgent — but it is dead weight in Drive.
4. **Optional:** three non-KeystoneOS tasks left enabled on the Windows box
   (`CFB-ForecastCaptureReminder`, `DailyGmailDigest`, `Refresh_All_Data`). None touch the
   shared repos.

## Traps that cost real time today

- `$(find ...)` word-splits on the space in "My Drive" — bit me three times. Use
  `-print0` / `read -r -d ''`.
- `du` on a DriveFS path reports *local cache*, not logical size. Compare file counts and
  `stat -f%z`.
- **Reading a Drive file materializes it**, so any scan warms the cache and a later run
  passes for reasons that will not hold after eviction.
- `pkill -f "^/usr/bin/rsync"` matches only the client; the `--server` child's `argv[0]` is
  bare `rsync`, so that pattern strands receivers. Match the destination path instead.
- A wedged rsync ignores SIGTERM. Only SIGKILL clears it.
- Reading an exit code through a pipe returns the last element's status.
